headline: Triple-B Hong Kong landlord in Causeway Bay has resilient recurring income but faces weak office cycle and capex-heavy development pipeline; supportive technicals have pushed valuation to unattractive levels, making it merely a good company rather than a good bond at this price
reasoning: The unnamed Hong Kong landlord holds strong assets in the high-traffic Causeway Bay precinct with resilient recurring income, providing adequate liquidity for several years. However the Hong Kong office market remains very weak, and the company plans new developments requiring significant capital expenditure. Limited bond supply supports technicals but has bid the valuation to levels where the spread no longer compensates for sitting through a weak office cycle and elevated capex period. For Liao, all three pillars — fundamentals, technicals and valuation — must align, and here valuation fails to clear the bar.
quote: So like right now, I'm looking at a Hong Kong property bond. It's a triple B rated landlord with strong assets and causeway base. So it's a high traffic area in Hong Kong. And it has like resilient recurring income. But the thing is like the office market in Hong Kong is still very weak. And this company still wants to build new developments. So to me, I'm thinking the company is actually okay, it's pretty decent, it's got enough liquidity for the next few years. But and on the technicals for this bond, there's limited supply. But because of this supportive technicals, the valuation is not cheap. So then it makes me think, is this just a good company? headline: Asian credit market is structurally healthier and higher quality post-2022 China property shock, with supportive net supply technicals likely to persist
reasoning: The collapse of China property as a major sector eliminated highly leveraged, land-appreciation-dependent issuers, shrinking the market but improving its quality composition. Simultaneously, rising US rates pushed Asian issuers to fund domestically, reducing offshore dollar supply further. These two forces combined to make the market more differentiated and higher quality. Liao expects the higher quality bias to persist, with the investment challenge now being picking the right bonds at the right spread.
quote: China property, or China real estate, wasn't just a big sector shock. It was like a big market structure shock to Asia credit. So for years, China property was a very large part of Asia credit. And what happened was that these companies were too reliant on leverage and land price appreciation. And pre-sales. So once regulations tightened and liquidity dried up, so all the buyer confidence weakened, sales slowed, and these companies defaulted, restructured, or stopped being investable. So that was a big change to the market. And on top of that, during that time in that year, US rates were going higher. So again, offshore funding was expensive for Asian companies in general. So they started issuing in their local domestic currencies and only came to the offshore market selectively. And what that did to the market was it shrank the supply. So the net supply became very supportive for the market. So those two things kind of led to the market being very different now. So I'd say it's healthier, it's differentiated, and it's overall much higher quality.
episode_title: Why Asian credit deserves a closer look

conviction: high conviction — regret at not sizing larger ('table pound')
headline: Regret not sizing larger at two separate entry points in 2023 and 2025; AI-driven high bandwidth memory demand structurally changed the company from a weak cyclical to a market leader, with fundamentals improving faster than market narrative
reasoning: In 2023, the market viewed SK Hynix as a boom-bust memory play after revenue fell 30% and losses mounted. Liao began buying the bonds at distressed spreads and they subsequently recovered through 2024. A second entry point appeared in 2025 when tariff concerns re-widened spreads. By that point the company had become structurally different: AI server demand had elevated high bandwidth memory (HBM) from a commodity to a critical, high-value product, and SK Hynix is the market leader in HBM. The lesson drawn was that when fundamentals are improving faster than the market narrative, position sizing should reflect that conviction.
quote: So maybe one of the lessons that stuck with me is on this company called SK Hynix. It's a Korean semiconductor company that makes advanced memory chips for our PCs, servers, phones, AI systems. And what happened here in 2023, the market saw it as a boom bust memory company. So memory prices had fallen hard, revenue was down 30%, and the company was making losses. So that's when we started to own the bond and it started to recover in 2024. But I didn't table pound it, so I owned it, but I didn't table pound it. And that kind of led me to miss out on these outsized returns. So in 2025, the entry point came again because of tariffs. So the bond spread sort of widened. That provided another entry point. One more chance, but I didn't table pound. That was the regret because it was so unstable in the market then. And by then, the company had become a completely different company, a much stronger company. It wasn't just a weak cyclical company. AI demand had sort of changed high end memory. And this is like a market leader in high bandwidth memory. That's critical memory for AI servers.

He draws explicit parallels to the railway boom of the 1840s and the TMT bubble of the late 1990s, where similar financial innovations funded massive capital expenditure that ultimately destroyed investor returns.

There's not a lot of cash changing hands, so a lot of promises, IOUs, the use of options and vendor paper, all of which is redeemable as an indeterminate date in the future based on a vision of a transformed and highly profitable new world.

headline: Neoclouds face same fate as alternative telecoms carriers in 2000 — no identifiable moats, uncertain ROI before hardware obsolescence, short seller Jim Chanos argues they will never earn cost of capital

headline: Division 296 now law: additional 15% tax on super earnings above $3M and 10% above $10M, effective from 30 June 2027 measurement date
reasoning: The Division 296 legislation was passed through Parliament in March 2026 after two years of debate. It imposes an additional 15% tax on the proportion of earnings attributable to superannuation balances exceeding $3 million, and a further 10% on balances exceeding $10 million, bringing effective tax rates to 30% and 40% respectively on those proportions. The thresholds will be CPI-indexed at certain increments. The first measurement year is transitional, with balances assessed at 30 June 2027; from 1 July 2027 onwards, the higher of the opening or closing balance for the financial year determines whether a member is subject to the tax. The tax is levied on the individual rather than the fund, so members can elect to pay it personally or have their super fund pay it, providing cash flow flexibility.
quote: Division 296 will apply to individuals that have total superannuation balances at the start of the financial year or at the end of the financial year that exceeds $3 million. However, there is good news, the 2026-2027 financial year is a transitional year for division 296 purposes. What that means is in the first year, the total super balance will be in reference to the members closing balance as at 30 June 2027. So, if at 30 June 2027, a member across all the superannuation interest has a balance less than $3 million, they won't be subject to the division 296 tax.
episode_title: $3 million super tax - what you need to know - post 1 July 2026

reasoning: Net issuance for long-maturity bonds from non-AI corporates contracted materially in 2025 and year-to-date, which could initially appear to be crowding out. However, corporate borrowers are not passive takers of the maturity structure; they actively time issuance, favouring shorter maturities when long-dated yields are elevated. The academic literature supports this: companies adjust the duration of supply in response to government changes in duration pricing. The contraction in long-end issuance therefore reflects rational corporate finance decisions under a high long-yield environment, not hyperscaler-specific displacement.

For them, this maturity choice is a real corporate finance decision shaped by the trade-off between locking and funding and preserving flexibility. The academic literature also shows that, at the aggregate level, corporate borrowers have tended to adjust the amount of duration they supply when the government changes the amount or price of duration in the market. Simply put, companies manage duration actively, so a decline in long-end issuance does not automatically mean they have been crowded out, especially in the current environment where long-dated yields have risen materially.

headline: Developed market rates still offer persistent inefficiency despite 30 years of arbitrage, with current environment of policy experimentation and fragmented buyer base making it an especially rich moment

The current environment — where the traditional bond buyers (Japan, China, the Fed via QE) have stepped back and the Treasury is experimenting with buybacks and duration management — creates new dislocations. With 43 instruments describing the same rate process in the first three years of the curve, not everything is priced efficiently on any given day.

We thought, well, base this trade until we can't base this trade. Here we are. I would have expected things to become more efficient over time. But instead, we have better tools, a better team with more experience, more diversity of perspectives, better path to this moment. We can aggregate a lot of information across the portfolio. We can have a pair of a US dollar bond and another currency. Same obligor, often defaulted, often cross defaulted under competent jurisdiction. So it's something to be considered very, very carefully if you're looking down that option. And in my view, it's not really workable because of risks like that.

headline: The 52-week high is an irrational anchor: professional investors buy what retail investors sell near that level
reasoning: Andrew Coleman argues that the 52-week high is an arbitrary number with no fundamental significance — it simply measures the highest price over a trailing year with no basis in company value. Despite this, it exerts strong psychological power through anchoring and reference dependence, causing everyday investors to feel uncomfortable and want to sell when a stock approaches that level. He notes that professionals tend to be on the other side of those trades, happily buying what retail sells. He frames this as a classic rational-actor versus human-behaviour split, driven by heuristics and gut feelings rather than rigorous analysis.
quote: The 52 week high is just a number. So why does it hold power over us? It's a great question, right? Because rationally it shouldn't. I mean, if you theoretically believe, as we all, I presume, watching this show do, which is that the good companies over time will rise in price and the poor companies will fall, then simply arbitrarily measuring from one date to another 52 weeks apart and saying the high within that period means anything, of course, is irrational. It means absolutely nothing. But I think it's a fascinating thing about how we as humans interact... the rational actor does things mathematically and does them rationally and considered and researched and rigorous. And then the humans do things with heuristics, rules of thumb. We get gut feelings. And I think the 52 week high ends up playing on a few of those, but in particular, the concept of anchoring.

headline: Anchoring bias driven by evolutionary scarcity psychology; trading platforms amplify it by always showing the purchase price rather than intrinsic value

In the stock market, this manifests as anchoring on the purchase price rather than intrinsic or relative value. Trading software reinforces this by displaying the price paid every time an investor logs in. Brokerages benefit from this bias because it encourages more trading, generating commission revenue regardless of portfolio outcomes. The rational alternative is to anchor on intrinsic value or a relevant valuation ratio such as P/E, not the nominal price paid.

headline: Disposition effect drives retail selling at highs: investors lock in gains without knowing fundamental value, using price paid as their only reference point
reasoning: Andrew Grant explains that the disposition effect — the tendency to sell winners and hold losers — is the primary driver of retail selling near 52-week highs. Investors anchor to their purchase price; when the current price exceeds it, the impulse is to lock in the gain. The flip side is 'get-even-itis', where investors hold losing positions waiting to recover to break-even. He emphasises that retail investors lack the valuation tools to judge whether a price is fundamentally cheap or expensive, so they rely on the 52-week range as a crude barometer, using it as a sell signal without any fundamental basis.
quote: One of the most common ways in which people make decisions is I bought the stock at a price, and now it's currently worth more than what I paid for it. So this is something called the disposition effect. It means I want to sell the stock because I'm going to lock in this game, right? So making a profit, that seems to be what we're all aiming for in the stock price... what we don't know when it comes to trading stocks and what individual investors aren't really good at is understanding how much should the stock be worth, right? The stock could be worth $32 on the stock market. I'm like, is that a good price? Is that a bad price? I don't know, right. All I can say is it's worth more than what I paid for. And I can see relative to where the stock's been over the past year here. It's at a high price time to sell. So that's the logic. It's like the barometer the temperature. headline: Individual investors consistently mistimed — buying after runs and replacing sold stocks with ones that go up even more; doing the opposite of the crowd may offer an edge
reasoning: Andrew Grant notes that individual investors lack the full information set and analytical capability of professional investors, leaving them working with limited data. Behavioural finance research shows retail investors are poor at timing: they tend to buy stocks that have already risen too much, and when they sell, they replace those positions with stocks that subsequently appreciate even further. This implies a contrarian signal — buying what individuals want to sell and selling what they want to buy may generate excess returns. The utility derived from selling at a profit also reinforces the disposition effect, making investors reluctant to sell at a loss even when it would be rational.
quote: Research in behavioral finance shows that individuals aren't good at timing their decisions. Right. So in other words, they'll buy stocks after they've gone up too much. And then they'll replace stocks in their portfolio with stocks then end up going up even more. So it ends up that if you followed what the individual does and do the exact opposite, so you buy the stocks they want to sell and you sell the stocks they want to buy, there's probably some likelihood of earning a profit.

He warns that 'bad loans are written in good times' and that managers overexposed to individual developers with poor leverage and cash-flow disciplines are now facing consequences. ASIC surveillance and enforcement actions are ongoing, which he views as a positive clearing-out for the sector overall.
quote: As a lender, you are always preparing for a downturn. Or at least you should be. And our concern is we're looking at the market now is there seems to be what is a pretty straightforward situation where a developer in the western suburbs of Sydney has gotten itself into trouble... bad loans are written in good times. So when you look at a situation where you've got a slowing property market, what you do see is those lenders who've been building really good quality, diversified portfolios around high quality assets. headline: USD structural debasement thesis: financial repression and sustained negative real yields are the only politically viable exit from a fiscal debt trap, making the dollar the pressure valve
reasoning: The US has a spending problem compounded by politically entrenched entitlements (social security, federal health, veterans' benefits) and interest payments that already consume 98.4% of annual tax receipts and are growing at a 5.7% CAGR — far exceeding the CBO's 3.9% nominal GDP growth forecast. Austerity is politically impermissible and defaulting on debt would destroy bond markets. The only viable path is financial repression: pinning nominal rates below inflation to erode the real debt burden, as the US did from 1945–1980. Under the current floating dollar regime, the currency must absorb this adjustment. Historical data from the IMF and Reinhart & Rogoff shows roughly 80% of net-debtor countries with debt/GDP above 120% suffered a sovereign default, inflation crisis, or currency crash within a decade. The fund is explicitly building a margin of safety in its global portfolio against USD exposure given this macro setup.
quote: The United States undoubtedly has a spending problem. Ultimately, this problem is compounded by a pernicious permission structure across the American political divide which optimises for short-term sugar hits like unfunded tax cuts, expanded entitlements and one-off transfers as band-aid workarounds to paper over the long-term cracks of the country's significantly deteriorating fiscal outlook... We believe any attempt at true austerity would significantly hurt U.S. equity markets whilst defaulting on debt would have a similar effect on the U.S. bond market. Given the mass citizen wealth tied up in U.S. equities and the widespread perception of U.S. paper as risk-free, we believe both options are, at their core, politically impermissible. This perfect storm affords the U.S. only one real avenue to veer from its disastrous fiscal trajectory. That is financial repression and sustained negative real yields by pinning nominal rates below inflation. Given today's floating U.S. dollar regime, the currency must be the valve to print their way out of this impending crisis.
episode_title: The Silent Threat of US Dollar Exposure

headline: Structurally bearish on the US dollar: applying a 10% per annum currency discount to all US-dollar-denominated earnings to reflect risk of fiscal repression leaking into a weaker exchange rate
reasoning: The fund argues that with US Debt-to-GDP above 120%, PPI inflation at 5.4%, the 10-year yield near 5%, and potential $1.2T in new stimulus (Trump's $5,000 adult dividend proposal), the US fiscal outlook is deteriorating rapidly. Under the current floating-dollar regime (unlike Bretton Woods), the Fed would need to monetise debt by printing dollars, causing structurally higher inflation and a weaker exchange rate. The firm expects a large share of foreign and domestic asset holders to diversify away from US dollars as this dynamic becomes clearer. To manage this risk without direct currency hedging, they apply a 10% per annum translation haircut to future earnings and free cash flow predominantly denominated in USD, and only invest after this adjustment if a stock still offers 75–100% upside over 2–3 years.
quote: To hedge against this risk, we have built a highly conservative margin of safety into our investment process. We apply a 10% per annum currency discount to our view of a business's future earnings power and free cash flow generation whereby the bulk of these earnings are denominated within the United States. To be clear, this haircut is not a view that these businesses will earn 10% less in U.S. dollar terms. Instead, it is a translation adjustment whereby we mark down the base-currency value of these U.S. dollar earnings by 10% per annum to reflect the risk that repression under a floating dollar regime will leak into a structurally weaker exchange rate. Crucially, this 10% is not a forecast. Instead, it is a deliberately conservative margin of safety that we believe is large enough to offer considerable downside protection for our portfolio.
episode_title: The Silent Threat of US Dollar Exposure

headline: AI represents genuine exponential change warranting a dedicated portfolio sleeve, even at high valuations, because the 10-year transformation potential justifies paying prices that would be indefensible in a normal environment
reasoning: Perold argues that AI-driven change is genuinely exponential and that high prices are actually consistent with things going very well. He recommends creating a dedicated AI sleeve to free oneself from constant cross-comparison with non-AI investments. He acknowledges the danger of 'this time is different' reasoning but believes it is warranted here. Even if only a quarter or half of the AI potential materialises, the outcome would still be profound. The key discipline is thinking long term and being comfortable holding high-priced assets in a way that would be irrational in a conventional environment.
quote: You're seeing companies with extraordinary earnings growth, high valuations. We're seeing venture investments in the many billions. 20 billion value, 5 billion before. How do you decide those? How do you think about investing in a world where the underlying fundamentals are changing very quickly but the price is very high? If the price was low, would you believe it was changing? Because the price is high, it's consistent with things going really well. When the price is high, you always recoil. Part of you needs to say something like, AI is going to work. Ten years from now, we'll be in a world we won't recognize. It may not be the case. That's possible. Maybe only half of that's possible. It's still profound. Maybe only a quarter is possible. It's still profound. If I think that's true, it means that I need to think long term and be comfortable owning things at high prices, knowing that in any normal investment environment, you'd never own them because this is different. Those are the most dangerous words in investing, saying this time is different. But this time is different.

headline: Blockchain smart contracts can prevent capital destruction in construction lending by enforcing payment covenants at the point of transaction rather than after insolvency
reasoning: Mitchell explains that in the Australian construction sector, when a builder collapses, the last one or two progress payments have typically already been spent across multiple sites, and subcontractors and suppliers beneath have not been paid. Traditional loan covenants that restrict use of funds can only be enforced through the courts, by which time the capital has already been dissipated. Smart contracts on blockchain enforce the rules in real time at the point of transaction, potentially preventing builders from trading while insolvent and protecting lenders and subcontractors from the cents-in-the-dollar outcomes common in construction insolvencies.
quote: Because typically when a builder goes under as, as anyone in the sector knows, they've been the last progress payment or the one and possibly the one before that, they're built in managing that across multiple sites. And it's likely that the subways and suppliers beneath haven't been paid. And, and this goes back to the point of our technology being able to enforce the rules around contracts in real time. So at the point of transaction, that's a brilliant part of smart contracts in blockchain tech because without that, you know, you can put it into a a contract, you can say the covenant says, you know, you can't use this in other, other projects. But by the time that that goes to be enforced in the courts, all the money's gone. You know, the capital's being torched, it's too late. So you're fighting over cents in the dollar in the courts rather than at the time of transaction that being enforced.

reasoning: Mitchell describes how his firm's technology sits between the movement of money in construction financing, mandating that developers and builders record every dollar in real time on a blockchain, creating a cryptographically signed, permanent, unbreakable and shareable record. He contrasts this with the current primitive back-office approach where duplicate paper receipts from two parties create a 'trust me' problem that banks cannot resolve due to privacy constraints. The technology also enforces contract covenants at the point of transaction via smart contracts, preventing, for example, developers from diverting restricted funds to other projects.

And what that means is that every single dollar spent on that project is not only it's permanent, unbreakable and shareable at source record that's created. headline: Data spending arms race has hit diminishing returns; real edge now lies in judgement, organisational speed and trust, not data spend
reasoning: Michael Skinner argues that global spending on market data and analysis has set records nearly every year for over a decade, yet active fund performance outcomes are dispersed and many active funds underperform benchmarks over ten years. He draws on the 1980 Grossman-Stiglitz theorem, which holds that information earns a return only while it is scarce. As AI is set to commoditise data further, the informational edge from data spending is eroding. Skinner concludes the real competitive advantage has shifted to judgement, organisational speed and trust rather than data expenditure.
quote: In the data arms race of investing, judgement has never been so important. In 1980, Sanford Grossman and Joseph Stiglitz published a paper with an inconvenient conclusion for anyone selling market data: information earns a return only while it is scarce. If share prices reflected all possible information and the efficient market hypothesis was true, nobody would be paid to do research, and alpha generation would be improbable, if not impossible. The market needs inefficiency to fund the people who make it efficient. Almost half a century later, the funds management industry is determined to test the theorem again. Global spending on market data and analysis has set a record nearly every year for more than a decade. Over roughly the same period, the performance scorecard is somewhat underwhelming: return outcomes are dispersed, and many active funds underperform their benchmark over ten years.
episode_title: Data and AI: Is the Data Arms Race Over?

headline: Passive investing amplifies momentum, allowing stocks to stay overpriced 6-12 months after index inclusion; best active opportunities are where forced buying exhausts itself or ahead of index adds in $300-500M cap names
reasoning: James Sioud explains that passive investing mechanically magnifies momentum: once a stock is added to indices, market participants are forced to buy it regardless of fundamentals, which can keep it expensive for 6 to 12 months. Unlike a decade ago, shorting an overpriced stock immediately at the point of inclusion is more dangerous because the momentum can run much longer. Instead, the best short ideas are where that forced-buying cycle has ended and the stock begins falling. On the long side, identifying companies in the $300-500 million market cap range where a fundamental thesis coincides with an upcoming index addition allows early entry before forced flows inflate the price.
quote: I think you just have to be honest with how passive investing works and it it's essentially a magnification of momentum. If a stock is going up, it tends to continue going up, especially when it gets added to indices. So a stock can easily get overpriced on fundamentals and stay that way for 612 months as it gets added. So various indices and as many market participants are forced to buy that company. Now maybe 10 years ago, you would short that company as it gets 10% or 30% too expensive. I think these days you have to be aware that this can run a lot longer and you have to be open to riding a momentum, but also being conscious that it will break eventually. So some of the best ideas we have are where that force buy in has run out and that stock's going to start falling. But also on the flip side, identifying companies around that 300 to $500 million market cap range where we form a fundamental view that can coincide side with an index add and allow us to get earlier in that journey before it gets too expensive and ultimately take advantage of that those forced flows in the market.

headline: Australian trust law and tax legislation riddled with holes — Division 296 flip-flopping, testamentary trust backflips, and an inadequate discretionary-to-fixed trust election mechanism that punishes mistakes permanently with no exemptions for death, divorce, fraud or elder abuse

The proposed fix — an election to convert discretionary trusts into fixed trusts to avoid state stamp duty on restructuring — is described as totally inadequate and potentially worse than the problem it solves. Most critically, if a trustee makes a distribution that deviates from the fixed election, the CGT exemption is lost permanently with no carve-outs for death, divorce, fraud, elder abuse or loss of capacity. Shorte labels this year's output 'Swiss cheese legislation' and expects industry associations to return to Treasury with a long list of missed issues.
quote: Look, I'm tired of, you know, the government rushing out changes in legislation and then having to fix holes in it. You know, we, we saw this with the Division 296, you know, unrealized gains in unrealized gains out indexation in indexation out. You know, it's now we're seeing with the, these changes to trust law, first the, the testamentary trusts were going to be included in these changes. Now they're, they're not. And then they've brought in this election to basically turn the trust from a discretionary trust basically into a fixed trust to try and avoid the problems with any restructuring causing stamp duty and other taxes with, with the states. But you know, the, the first initial look at their, at their fix is that it's, it's totally inadequate. And it's probably going to mean that even more people may get hit with stamp state stamp duty if they do any changes in the restructuring. So, yeah, and and you know, it's really draconian. You do you take this election to do fixed distributions for the future. And if you make, if you make a mistake or you make a, a the wrong distribution, not in line with those, you lose the exemption for, for life. There's no going back. So it's a you, you can't fix it. But that means that something like a death, a divorce, someone that had been subject to fraud, elder abuse, loss of capacity, all of those things would you would usually think would be built into the legislation as exemptions if something, you know, happened. None of that's been mentioned. So again, we're going to probably see all the associations going back to the Treasury and going you miss this, this and this, get your acting gear. So I'm calling this year's taxes and legislation the Swiss cheese legislation because they're full of holes.

He suggests the sweet spot for producers and consumers is $60-70 per barrel. Below $80 the macroeconomic impact is limited, but above $90-100 it becomes inflationary and weighs on consumer spending. With Brent above $96, he says the world is firmly in the uncomfortable zone, with the outcome dependent on how the US-Iran conflict evolves.
quote: Energy obviously drives most economies as a, as an input cost. Now some, you know, some economies more than others, but ultimately almost everything that we do and use has an oil link to it. So a higher oil price is obviously going to drive inflation, not just about the cost of petrol for cars, but also, you know, plastics, food distribution, all kinds of things. So oil that, you know, the sweet spot for oil in terms of production, in terms of supply in terms of consumers is probably 60 to $70 a barrel. You know, if you get under, if it's still under 80, you're probably not making much difference. But once you start getting over 90 to 100, it does start to have an effect from an inflationary endpoint point of view as well as a consumer spending point of view. So so that we're definitely in the uncomfortable period of, of, of of sort of oil prices being where they are.

headline: A really good business can produce disappointing returns if priced for perfection; a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if expectations were excessively pessimistic
reasoning: Investing is not a simple mathematical formula where good fundamentals mechanically produce good returns. What matters is how a company's earnings and fundamentals compare to the collective expectations already embedded in the share price. A high-quality company whose strong performance is already anticipated will see a stagnant or disappointing share price — as illustrated by employees who receive company shares and cannot understand why strong earnings produce no price gain. Conversely, a mediocre business can outperform if market expectations were excessively negative. This is the game-theory dimension of investing: outcomes depend not just on fundamentals but on the decisions and perceptions of all other market participants.
quote: And we're not saying that company earnings and other fundamentals don't matter. They of course do. But, it also matters how they compare to everyone else's expectations. And that really matters in terms of the outcome that you will achieve. So, really good business can produce disappointing investment returns if it's priced for perfection. On the other hand, a mediocre company can generate excellent returns if those expectations were excessively pessimistic.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

headline: Extreme pessimism in April 2025 tariff turmoil drove herd selling via loss aversion, while extreme optimism fuels bubble-buying — both are prisoner's-dilemma dynamics that destroy investor returns
reasoning: During the April 2025 tariff turmoil, investor sentiment surveys and the put/call ratio showed extreme pessimism, leading investors to sell en masse to avoid being 'left holding the bag.' This is driven by loss aversion — losses feel twice as painful as equivalent gains — causing selling that begets more selling. The mirror dynamic occurs in bubbles, where investors buy not because prices are justified but because they expect someone else to pay even more tomorrow. The key insight is that this behaviour doesn't require irrationality; it simply requires investors responding to their perception of the incentives they face. The optimal path — analogous to both prisoners staying silent — is for investors to remain patient during corrections, focus on fundamentals, and avoid portfolio decisions based on anticipating what everyone else will do.
quote: And what we see in the graph is extreme pessimism that often leads to large dips in the index where investors clamor to remove themselves before others do. They don't want to be the ones that are left holding the bag. And this is an example of the concept of loss aversion where a loss feels twice as painful as an equivalent gain. And then on the other side of that, of course, is when there's extreme optimism and that is when investors are trying to get into the market to capitalize on gains that they foresee before others do that. Now, imagine a world where more investors remain patient during a market correction. Share prices would likely recover much quicker and everyone would benefit. But instead, what we actually see in real life is that many investors sell because they fear others are going to sell and they're trying to get out of the market first.
episode_title: Why Smart Investors Still Lose Money

The ATO allows six months to restructure a fund following a member's death. His key advice is to simplify the SMSF and put succession structures in place while all members still have full capacity.
quote: So there's a couple of things to think about South. All members of the supplemented super fund should know a few things about it. Now, quite often you do find that one member of the fund is, is kind of the chief financial officer of the fund, if you like, who's looking after everything to do with it. They know when the tax is due, they know when the audit's happening, they're paying the all the bills out of the fund. And then maybe one or two or three of the other members don't really take an active role. But it's very important that everybody understands a few things about their funds. First of all, who is the trustee? Do you have an individual trustee structure or corporate trustee structure? Because that makes a difference at the end of the day if you have to. If you have a member pass away or become incapable of running the fund, looking at who has power of attorney over the members of the fund as well. And, and remembering that holding an enduring power between it doesn't automatically make somebody else the trustee if they take over from you. But then we need to have that process in place. It's important for everyone to know who's getting the benefit, the binding death dominations, how that all works when someone was to pass away and what's going to happen to the assets within the fund.
